newsitem.title: UK: UK transport policy paper due this week-sources.
newsitem.headline: UK transport policy paper due this week-sources.

text.p: Britain's government is set to reignite the debate on the transportation gridlock with the release this week of its integrated transport consultative document, industry sources said.
The document will set the parameters for change and has a sweeping remit which will impact on the multi-billion pound automotive, rail and bus industries.
The key issues covered by the paper could include an overhaul of regulation of the rail and bus industries, local transport funding, road pricing, freight and road safety.

"If the government is serious about its wider objective to reduce congestion on roads it needs to do more than tinker with the mess inherited from the Tories (Conservatives)," said Jonathan Bray of passenger group Save Our Railways (SOR).

Transport industry sources told Reuters they had been told the document's release was pencilled in for Thursday, with a release by the end of the month at the latest. But the Department of Transport refused to comment. The document will lead to a White Paper due out early next year.
Since taking office, Labour has pledged to overhaul rail regulation, increase rail and bus usage and discourage the use of cars.
One of the key measures in this week's paper will be plans for the new Strategic Rail Authority to govern the trains.

"The new Labour government needs to use its proposed Strategic Rail Authority to take radical measures to ensure the railway subsidies (given to private operators) produce a modern and high quality railway," said SOR's Bray.
The key question is how this will impact on existing rail regulators -- Opraf, which governs the franchise terms of the 25 train operating companies (TOCS), and the Office of the Rail Regulator.
Both regulators have recently been seen toughening up on errant rail operators as their political future hangs in the balance.

Rail operators will be looking to see if the government tightens rail regulation in the first review since Labour took power from the Conservatives who were responsible for privatising rail and buses.
Buses could also see a clampdown on errant operators, said Lynn Sloman, director of Transport 2000, the lobby group which has been in regular talks with ministers.
"We expect something on how to enforce 'quality partnerships' between local authorities and bus operators," Sloman told Reuters.

"At present local authorities work with some bus operators to provide bus priority in traffic lanes and other benefits in return for quality frequent-running, low emission services being run," she said.
But the government fears that some operators are not meeting their side of the bargain. "The paper will want to enforce those partnerships," Sloman said.
The creation of more priority bus lanes at the expense of car lanes is also a possibility.
"The government wishes to re-allocate road space," Sloman said.

She added that Transport 2000 has sent out a "very strong and very clear" message on the need for a transport tax which includes "a non-residential parking or road pricing tax where the revenues are ring-fenced for local transport spending".
Friends of the Earth, the environmental pressure group, is also backing measures to control car usage though it favours higher fuel taxation.
FOE's Roger Higman told Reuters he would also like to see more specific long-term targets set in stone.
"We want targets for traffic to be cut by 10 percent by the year 2000 and in the meantime low cost measures to boost public transport and cycling."
Road pricing is one route which could be used to raise funds for public transport and cut car usage simultaneously.
But the details of how road-pricing could work is still under debate. A pilot project is underway in Leicester.
Lesser measures in the consultative document are expected to include proposals to improve road safety and a possible cap on lorry weight at 40 tonnes.
